microtopics.title: Path travelled is not start-to-finish change
microtopics.badge_reason: Everyday language often uses distance for both ideas, so an out-and-back case is needed to force the distinction.
entry_assumptions: Can trace a route from a marked start to a marked finish on a straight line.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Distance counts the whole route travelled, while displacement records only the directed change from start to finish; a return to the start leaves zero displacement after a nonzero journey.

teaching_path.action: Mark a start point on a straight path and declare east as the positive direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: A directed change is only readable once the line has a stated positive way.
teaching_path.output: start: S.  east: positive.  west: opposite.

teaching_path.action: Trace a walk away from S and then back to S, counting every part of the route.
teaching_path.why_valid: The route count accumulates what was travelled even though the final place can match the initial place.
teaching_path.output: route travelled: nonzero.  start-to-finish change: zero because finish = S.

teaching_path.action: Compare that return trip with a one-way trip chosen to have the same total route length.
teaching_path.why_valid: Holding route length fixed while changing the finish isolates the information displacement carries.
teaching_path.output: same route length; different finish -> different displacement.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Distance travelled and displacement are always the same number.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A walker leaves a marker, turns around, and finishes back at the marker. Is the journey length zero just because the final change in position is zero?
misconceptions.repair: Count every part of the route for distance; compare only the start and finish for displacement, keeping the declared direction.

exit_task.prompt: Route A leaves a marker and returns to it. Route B travels the same total amount but ends away from the marker. Without calculating a value, compare their distance and displacement.

answer.summary: The routes can have the same distance, but Route A has zero displacement while Route B has a nonzero directed displacement.
reasoning: Distance follows the whole route, so equal total travel can give equal distance.
Displacement compares only the finish with the start.
Returning to the marker erases the start-to-finish change, not the travelled route.
answer.check: Ignore the middle of each route and look only at the two endpoints; only Route A has matching endpoints.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The response makes only qualitative zero/nonzero and same/different comparisons; it asserts no computed magnitude.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created controlled contrast built from the committed matrix. Candidate packet material was consulted only as non-authoritative input.

predict.prompt: A person walks away from a marker and later returns exactly to it. Before naming any quantities, has every measure of the journey returned to zero?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The start-to-finish change is zero, but the travelled route is still nonzero.

attempt.produces: Two short descriptions of the same return trip: one that records the whole route and one that records only start versus finish.

rubric.criterion: The whole-route description remains nonzero.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeping travelled path information after the return.

rubric.criterion: The start-versus-finish description is zero.
rubric.evidence_of: Using endpoints rather than retracing the route for displacement.

accepted: 'The traveller covered a nonzero route, but finished where they started, so the endpoint change is zero.'
rejected: 'Both are zero because the traveller ended where they began.' This erases the path that was actually travelled.

route.ask: Did the traveller move along any part of the path before returning?
route.why_this_ask: It makes the existence of travelled path undeniable before the endpoint comparison is introduced.

route.ask: Where is the finish compared with the start?
route.why_this_ask: It switches from the history of the route to the endpoint relation.

route.ask: Which description should keep the detour: the whole route or the start-to-finish change?
route.why_this_ask: The learner has to assign the two pieces of information to different quantities rather than memorize names.

route.ask: If another route has the same total travel but ends elsewhere, which description must change?
route.why_this_ask: The comparison tests whether the endpoint information has actually been separated from path length.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path labels the two descriptions after a constructed return trip. The learner route first notices the contradiction between real travel and a zero endpoint change, then assigns each description a job.

boundary_test.prompt: If the traveller never leaves the starting marker, what happens to both descriptions?
boundary_test.answer: Both are zero: there is no travelled route and no change between start and finish.
boundary_test.confirms: The two quantities can agree in a boundary case without becoming the same concept.

microtopics.title: Zero velocity at an instant does not mean zero acceleration
microtopics.badge_reason: A single still-looking instant invites learners to confuse the current velocity with how velocity is changing.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish the direction of motion just before and just after a turning point.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Velocity and acceleration answer different questions: velocity can be zero at one instant while a nonzero acceleration determines the change through that instant.

teaching_path.action: Record three moments around a vertical turning point: just before the top, at the top, and just after.
teaching_path.why_valid: A single snapshot hides change; neighbouring moments reveal whether the zero-velocity state persists.
teaching_path.output: before: moving upward.  top: velocity zero.  after: moving downward.

teaching_path.action: Compare the direction of the velocity change across those three moments.
teaching_path.why_valid: Going from upward through zero to downward requires the velocity to keep changing through the top instant.
teaching_path.output: velocity change through the top: downward, including at the zero-velocity instant.

teaching_path.action: Contrast the turning point with an object that is simply resting on a shelf.
teaching_path.why_valid: Both can have zero velocity now, but only one immediately changes velocity, so zero velocity alone cannot determine acceleration.
teaching_path.output: turning point: zero velocity with continuing change.  shelf: zero velocity with no motion change in the comparison.

teaching_path.action: Use v=0 only as the event condition for the vertical turning point while keeping the signed gravitational acceleration nonzero in the same instant.
teaching_path.why_valid: Velocity describes the instantaneous state of motion; acceleration describes how that velocity is changing. At the apex the upward velocity has just decreased to zero and immediately continues toward negative values under the same downward acceleration.
teaching_path.output: apex event: v=0 at one instant; acceleration remains downward, so +up gives a=-g and +down gives a=+g

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If velocity is zero at an instant, acceleration must also be zero at that instant.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: At the highest point of a vertically thrown object, velocity is momentarily zero. Does the next moment have the same velocity?
misconceptions.repair: Compare moments immediately before and after the top; the velocity changes from upward to downward, so acceleration remains nonzero through the zero-velocity instant.

exit_task.prompt: Two objects have zero velocity at one instant: one is at the top of a vertical flight, the other is resting on a shelf. What can you conclude about their accelerations from velocity alone?

answer.summary: Nothing definite from the zero velocity alone. The turning object can have nonzero downward acceleration while the resting object can have zero acceleration in the stated comparison.
reasoning: Velocity describes motion at the instant.
Acceleration describes how velocity is changing through the instant.
Neighbouring moments distinguish the turning point from sustained rest.
answer.check: Look immediately before and after the instant: a changing velocity signals nonzero acceleration even when the middle velocity is zero.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer distinguishes zero/nonzero acceleration qualitatively and gives no computed acceleration value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created turning-point contrast. It does not promote the candidate packet's quantitative projectile or kinematic equations.

predict.prompt: At the very top of a vertical throw the object is momentarily not moving upward or downward. Before reading on, do you predict its acceleration is also zero there?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Its velocity is zero only at that instant while its velocity is still changing from upward to downward.

attempt.produces: A three-moment before/top/after description plus a separate statement about the direction of the velocity change.

rubric.criterion: The top moment is labelled zero velocity without extending that zero to the neighbouring moments.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating the top as an instant rather than an interval of rest.

rubric.criterion: The velocity change is described as continuing downward through the top.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeping acceleration separate from the current velocity value.

accepted: 'Before: upward; top: zero; after: downward. The velocity is changing downward through all three moments.'
rejected: 'At the top both velocity and acceleration are zero because the object stops.' This treats an instant as a period of rest.

route.ask: Just before the top, which way is the object moving?
route.why_this_ask: The learner starts from an observable direction rather than a definition.

route.ask: Just after the top, which way is it moving?
route.why_this_ask: The second neighbour exposes the sign change that a single top snapshot hides.

route.ask: Can velocity change from upward to downward without changing through the middle instant?
route.why_this_ask: It forces the learner to reason about change rather than equate zero velocity with zero acceleration.

route.ask: How is this different from an object that remains on a shelf before and after the same instant?
route.why_this_ask: The contrast tests whether the learner can separate current velocity from its change.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path states the three moments and compares them. The learner route commits to the neighbouring directions first, then has to explain how the middle instant can be zero without ending the change.

boundary_test.prompt: An object is at rest before, during, and after the instant under discussion. Does zero velocity now still force a nonzero acceleration?
boundary_test.answer: No. With velocity unchanged at zero across the interval, this comparison supports zero acceleration.
boundary_test.confirms: The claim is not that zero velocity implies nonzero acceleration; it is that zero velocity alone does not decide acceleration.

microtopics.title: Average speed and average velocity come from different totals
microtopics.badge_reason: The arithmetic is simple, but equal-distance and equal-time weighting are easily confused.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish total travelled path from signed displacement and can read one positive elapsed interval.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Average speed divides total path length by total time, while average velocity divides signed displacement by that same time; neither is obtained by averaging listed speeds unless the weighting justifies it.

teaching_path.action: For one two-leg trip, record total path length, signed start-to-finish displacement, and the total elapsed time in separate rows.
teaching_path.why_valid: The two averages differ only in the numerator, so separating the totals prevents path and endpoint information from being merged.
teaching_path.output: distance_total = sum of leg lengths; Delta x = x_final - x_initial; Delta t = total elapsed time.

teaching_path.action: Divide total path length by total time, then divide signed displacement by the same total time.
teaching_path.why_valid: Each relation is a total-over-common-interval average and the gate owns both formulas.
teaching_path.output: speed_avg = distance_total / Delta t; v_avg = Delta x / Delta t.

teaching_path.action: Check a return trip where the finish equals the start.
teaching_path.why_valid: The boundary keeps nonzero path length while forcing displacement to zero, so it tests whether the two averages stayed distinct.
teaching_path.output: return trip -> average speed may be nonzero; whole-trip average velocity = 0.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Average speed is always the arithmetic mean of the speeds listed for the trip.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two equal-distance legs are travelled at different speeds. Did the traveller spend equal time at each speed?
misconceptions.repair: Build total distance and total time first. Only equal time weighting permits an unweighted arithmetic mean of speeds.

exit_task.prompt: A trip covers 120 m of total path, finishes 40 m in the positive direction from its start, and lasts 20 s. Find the average speed and average velocity.

answer.summary: Average speed is 6 m/s and average velocity is +2 m/s.
reasoning: Average speed uses 120 m / 20 s = 6 m/s.
Average velocity uses the signed displacement +40 m / 20 s = +2 m/s.
The different numerators explain why the two averages differ.
answer.check: Both calculations use the same 20 s interval; only the path-versus-displacement numerator changes.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created average-rate construction bound to gate-owned relations and an implemented Physics validator.

predict.prompt: A traveller returns to the starting point after moving for a nonzero time. Must average speed and average velocity both be zero?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Whole-trip displacement and average velocity are zero, but total path length and average speed can be nonzero.

attempt.produces: Separate distance, displacement and time totals followed by the two average-rate calculations.

rubric.criterion: Average speed uses total path length rather than displacement.
rubric.evidence_of: Preserving the distance/displacement distinction in the numerator.

rubric.criterion: Average velocity uses signed displacement and the same total time.
rubric.evidence_of: Using a common interval and retaining direction.

rejected: (speed on leg 1 + speed on leg 2)/2 without first establishing equal time weighting.

route.ask: What total quantity keeps every travelled leg even if the direction reverses?
route.why_this_ask: It recovers the path-length numerator.

route.ask: What signed quantity depends only on start and finish?
route.why_this_ask: It recovers the displacement numerator.

route.ask: Which elapsed time belongs under both totals?
route.why_this_ask: The two averages must use the same interval.

route.ask: What happens to each average on a return trip?
route.why_this_ask: The boundary checks that the two numerators were not conflated.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path constructs the two averages directly; the learner route starts from the return-trip conflict and reconstructs which total belongs to each rate.

boundary_test.prompt: If the traveller never leaves the start during a positive time interval, what are both averages?
boundary_test.answer: Both are zero because both total distance and signed displacement are zero while elapsed time is positive.
boundary_test.confirms: The two rates can agree without being the same quantity.

microtopics.title: Derive the constant-acceleration equations from one velocity-time graph
microtopics.badge_reason: The algebra is elementary, but the learner must connect graph slope and geometric area to three equivalent kinematic equations while preserving the model condition.
entry_assumptions: Can read a velocity-time graph, calculate a segment slope, and calculate rectangle, triangle and trapezoid areas.
Can distinguish a constant-slope velocity-time segment from a curved changing-acceleration segment.
microtopics.inferential_jump: One straight velocity-time segment carries all three Grade 9 kinematic equations: its slope gives v = u + at, its rectangle-plus-triangle area gives s = ut + 0.5at^2, and combining trapezoid area with the slope relation eliminates time to give v^2 = u^2 + 2as.

teaching_path.action: Read the straight velocity-time graph from (0,u) to (t,v) and identify one constant slope.
teaching_path.why_valid: A straight velocity-time segment means one acceleration value describes the whole interval.
teaching_path.output: slope = (v-u)/t = a; graph area = signed displacement s.

teaching_path.action: Rearrange the straight-line slope equation.
teaching_path.why_valid: The graph slope is the constant acceleration for the interval.
teaching_path.output: a = (v-u)/t -> a t = v-u -> v = u + a t.

teaching_path.action: Split the graph area into the initial-velocity rectangle and the acceleration triangle, then substitute v-u = a t.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-CONSTANT-ACCELERATION-GRAPH-AREA owns the displacement area and the two regions exactly partition it.

teaching_path.action: Write the same graph area as a trapezoid, substitute t = (v-u)/a from the slope, and factor the difference of squares.
teaching_path.why_valid: Both equations describe the same straight graph interval, so the common time variable can be eliminated.

teaching_path.action: Replace the straight segment with a curved velocity-time trace and ask whether the same graphical derivation is exact over the whole interval.
teaching_path.why_valid: A curved trace has changing slope, so one constant a no longer describes the interval and the straight-line rectangle/triangle construction is not the exact graph.
teaching_path.output: curved v-t trace -> changing a -> the constant-a graphical derivation does not apply exactly to the whole interval.

teaching_path.action: For bounded vertical motion in a region where local gravitational acceleration can be treated as constant, choose one positive vertical direction and translate the downward gravitational acceleration into one signed constant a before using any kinematic equation; do not change the sign of a when the velocity reverses.
teaching_path.why_valid: The sign of acceleration is set by the declared coordinate axis and the physical downward direction of gravity, not by whether the object is currently moving upward or downward.
teaching_path.output: +up -> a=-g; +down -> a=+g, where g>0 is the local acceleration magnitude; v may change sign while a keeps the same signed value over the constant-g interval

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The constant-acceleration equations are independent formulas to memorize rather than consequences of one straight velocity-time graph.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If the velocity-time graph is curved, can the same rectangle-plus-triangle derivation still use one constant a for the whole interval?
misconceptions.repair: Return to the graph: slope must be constant. Derive the equations from that slope and the graph area before using them.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Gravitational acceleration is -g while the object rises and +g after it starts falling.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If +up is fixed for the whole trip, did the physical direction of gravity reverse when the object's velocity changed from upward to downward?
misconceptions.repair: No. Keep the chosen axis fixed. With +up, gravity remains a=-g throughout the bounded flight; only velocity changes sign at the turning point.

exit_task.prompt: A velocity-time graph is a straight segment from 5 m/s at t = 0 to 11 m/s at t = 3 s. Use the graph slope to identify a, use its rectangle-plus-triangle area to find displacement, and show how the same graph yields v = u + at, s = ut + 0.5at^2, and v^2 = u^2 + 2as.

answer.summary: The slope gives a = 2 m/s^2 and v = u + at. The graph area is 15 m + 9 m = 24 m, giving s = ut + 0.5at^2. The trapezoid form combined with t = (v-u)/a gives v^2 = u^2 + 2as.
reasoning: Slope: a = (11-5)/3 = 2 m/s^2, so a = (v-u)/t rearranges to v = u + at.
Rectangle area: u t = 5 x 3 = 15 m.
Triangle area: 0.5(v-u)t = 0.5 x 6 x 3 = 9 m, so s = 24 m; substituting v-u = at gives s = ut + 0.5at^2.
The same area is s = 0.5(u+v)t. Substitute t=(v-u)/a: 2as=(u+v)(v-u)=v^2-u^2, hence v^2=u^2+2as.
answer.check: The direct displacement validator gives 24 m, and 11^2 = 5^2 + 2 x 2 x 24 = 121.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created Grade 9 graphical derivation bound to a data-backed velocity-time representation, gate-owned graph-area relation, and executable validator.

predict.prompt: If a velocity-time graph is a straight rising line, which two graph features can generate equations before any formula is recalled?
predict.defensible_answer: Its slope gives acceleration and its signed area gives displacement.

attempt.produces: A slope derivation of v=u+at, a rectangle-plus-triangle derivation of s=ut+0.5at^2, and a trapezoid/elimination derivation of v^2=u^2+2as.

rubric.criterion: Derives the velocity equation from graph slope.
rubric.evidence_of: Writing a=(v-u)/t and rearranging rather than quoting v=u+at.

rubric.criterion: Derives the displacement equation from rectangle plus triangle area.
rubric.evidence_of: Writing s=ut+0.5(v-u)t and substituting v-u=at.

rubric.criterion: Eliminates time using the trapezoid area and slope relation.
rubric.evidence_of: Reaching 2as=(u+v)(v-u)=v^2-u^2 before the no-time equation.

accepted: slope -> v=u+at; graph area -> s=ut+0.5at^2; trapezoid plus slope -> v^2=u^2+2as.
rejected: Listing all three equations without connecting them to slope or graph area.

route.ask: What is the slope of the straight velocity-time segment?
route.why_this_ask: It recovers the acceleration relation.

route.ask: What two simple shapes partition the area below that segment?
route.why_this_ask: It reconstructs displacement from geometry.

route.ask: How can the whole area also be written as one trapezoid?
route.why_this_ask: It supplies the form used to eliminate time.

route.ask: What fails if the graph is curved?
route.why_this_ask: It restores the constant-acceleration applicability condition.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path derives equations in order; the learner route starts from graph invariants—slope and area—and reconstructs why each algebraic form follows.

boundary_test.prompt: Can this exact straight-line graphical derivation be used unchanged on a curved velocity-time graph?
boundary_test.answer: No. A curved graph has changing slope, so one constant acceleration does not describe the whole interval.
boundary_test.confirms: The equations are derived under the constant-acceleration model rather than treated as universal identities.

microtopics.title: Uniform circular motion keeps speed while velocity turns
microtopics.badge_reason: Everyday use of 'speed' and 'velocity' can hide that direction change alone is a velocity change.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish speed from directed velocity and can recognize acceleration as a change of velocity.
microtopics.inferential_jump: An object moving around a circle at constant speed is still accelerating because velocity direction changes continuously; velocity is tangent, acceleration points inward, and the constant speed for one revolution is circumference divided by period: v = 2 pi r / T.

teaching_path.action: Mark equal-length velocity arrows tangent to a circle at several positions.
teaching_path.why_valid: Equal arrow length represents constant speed while tangent direction follows the instantaneous motion.
teaching_path.output: same speed; different tangent velocity directions.

teaching_path.action: Compare successive velocity arrows and identify the change in velocity direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: Velocity changes whenever either its magnitude or direction changes.
teaching_path.output: At two different points A and B: |v_A| = |v_B| = v, but v_A and v_B point in different tangent directions, so Delta v = v_B - v_A is nonzero.

teaching_path.action: Use symmetry at opposite points to check that the required acceleration is directed toward the centre rather than along the tangent.
teaching_path.why_valid: A tangential acceleration would change speed, while inward turning changes direction while preserving speed in the ideal uniform case.
teaching_path.output: uniform circular motion -> acceleration inward; velocity tangent.

teaching_path.action: For one complete uniform revolution, divide the circumference 2 pi r by the positive revolution period T.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-UNIFORM-CIRCULAR-SPEED is the gate-owned Grade 9 speed expression.
teaching_path.output: v = 2 pi r / T; for r = 7 m and T = 14 s, v = pi m/s ≈ 3.14 m/s.

misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A car moves around a circular track with a steady speedometer reading. Is its velocity unchanged?
misconceptions.repair: Compare the tangent directions at different points: the direction changes, so velocity changes and acceleration is nonzero.

exit_task.prompt: A runner moves uniformly around a circular track of radius 7 m and completes one revolution in 14 s. Find the speed, then state the qualitative directions of velocity and acceleration at any point.

answer.summary: The speed is pi m/s, about 3.14 m/s. Velocity is tangent to the circle in the direction of motion; acceleration points inward toward the centre.
reasoning: One revolution covers circumference 2 pi r = 14 pi m.
v = 14 pi m / 14 s = pi m/s ≈ 3.14 m/s.
Constant speed does not make velocity constant because its direction changes.
The velocity is tangent and the turning acceleration is inward.
answer.check: Doubling the period at the same radius would halve the speed, while the tangent/inward direction distinction remains.

predict.prompt: If a speedometer reading stays constant around a bend, is acceleration necessarily zero?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Velocity direction changes around the bend, so acceleration is nonzero even at constant speed.

attempt.produces: A one-revolution speed calculation plus tangent velocity and inward acceleration directions.

rubric.criterion: Uses circumference divided by revolution period for speed.
rubric.evidence_of: Applying the prescribed Grade 9 uniform-circular-speed expression.

rubric.criterion: Keeps velocity tangent and acceleration inward.
rubric.evidence_of: Separating speed magnitude from changing velocity direction.

accepted: r=7 m, T=14 s -> v=pi m/s ≈3.14 m/s; velocity tangent, acceleration inward.
rejected: v = r/T, or zero acceleration solely because speed is constant.

route.ask: Has the speed changed?
route.why_this_ask: It holds magnitude fixed.

route.ask: Has the velocity direction changed?
route.why_this_ask: It exposes the remaining source of velocity change.

route.ask: Would a tangential acceleration keep the speed constant?
route.why_this_ask: It rules out the tangent as the uniform-case acceleration direction.

route.ask: What direction is symmetric toward the turning centre?
route.why_this_ask: It reconstructs inward acceleration.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path compares tangent velocity arrows; the learner route starts from constant speed and discovers why direction change still requires acceleration.

boundary_test.prompt: If the path becomes straight while speed remains constant, what happens to the turning acceleration?
boundary_test.answer: It vanishes in the straight constant-velocity limit.
boundary_test.confirms: The acceleration in uniform circular motion is tied to continuous change of direction.

microtopics.title: Motion graphs turn coordinate change into rate
microtopics.badge_reason: The arithmetic is simple, but graph height, slope, and physical motion are easily confused.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish position, velocity and acceleration and can compute an interval average rate from two values.
microtopics.inferential_jump: On a position-time graph, segment slope is average velocity over that interval; on a velocity-time graph, segment slope is average acceleration. Graph height and graph slope answer different physical questions.

teaching_path.action: Read the axis names, units and two plotted coordinates before describing the motion.
teaching_path.why_valid: A graph only acquires physical meaning through its labelled quantities and coordinate values.
teaching_path.output: position-time graph: horizontal t in s, vertical x in m; velocity-time graph: horizontal t in s, vertical v in m/s.

teaching_path.action: On the position-time graph, subtract two position coordinates and divide by their time separation.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-AVERAGE-VELOCITY is the gate-owned interval relation and the graph supplies Delta x and Delta t.
teaching_path.output: between (2 s, 4 m) and (4 s, 8 m): v_avg = (8 - 4)/(4 - 2) = +2 m/s.

teaching_path.action: On the velocity-time graph, subtract two velocity coordinates and divide by their time separation.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-AVERAGE-ACCELERATION is the gate-owned interval relation and the graph supplies Delta v and Delta t.
teaching_path.output: between (2 s, 3 m/s) and (4 s, 5 m/s): a_avg = (5 - 3)/(4 - 2) = +1 m/s^2.

teaching_path.action: Use horizontal segments as boundary checks.
teaching_path.why_valid: A horizontal position-time segment has zero position change, while a horizontal velocity-time segment has zero velocity change.
teaching_path.output: horizontal x-t -> v_avg = 0; horizontal v-t -> a_avg = 0.

Translate a symbolic vertical-motion description into a velocity-time graph or vice versa.
transfer_boundaries: Do not flip the sign of gravitational acceleration when velocity changes direction.
Do not treat v=0 at the apex as evidence that a=0.
Do not replace signed displacement by total distance when an equation uses displacement.
Do not treat the familiar near-Earth value of g as universal at all locations or heights.
Do not import two-dimensional projectile or variable-acceleration methods into this one-dimensional bounded context.
common_wrong_routes: Use +g on the way down and -g on the way up despite keeping one fixed axis.
Set both v and a to zero at the highest point.
Use total path length in place of signed displacement in a constant-acceleration equation.
Choose a negative time root because it satisfies the algebra without checking the represented future event.
Treat equal height on ascent and descent as equal velocity rather than equal speed with opposite directions.

questions.stem: Route A leaves a marker and returns to it. Route B travels the same total amount but ends away from the marker. Without calculating a value, compare their distance and displacement.

answer.summary: The routes can have the same distance, but Route A has zero displacement while Route B has a nonzero directed displacement.
reasoning: Distance follows the whole route, so equal total travel can give equal distance.
Displacement compares only the finish with the start.
Returning to the marker erases the start-to-finish change, not the travelled route.
answer.check: Ignore the middle of each route and look only at the two endpoints; only Route A has matching endpoints.

hints.text: Start by asking yourself: Did the traveller move along any part of the path before returning?
Count every part of the route for distance; compare only the start and finish for displacement, keeping the declared direction.

questions.stem: A trip covers 120 m of total path, finishes 40 m in the positive direction from its start, and lasts 20 s. Find the average speed and average velocity.

answer.summary: Average speed is 6 m/s and average velocity is +2 m/s.
reasoning: Average speed uses 120 m / 20 s = 6 m/s.
Average velocity uses the signed displacement +40 m / 20 s = +2 m/s.
The different numerators explain why the two averages differ.
answer.check: Both calculations use the same 20 s interval; only the path-versus-displacement numerator changes.

hints.text: Start by asking: What total quantity keeps every travelled leg even if the direction reverses?
Build total distance and total time first. Only equal time weighting permits an unweighted arithmetic mean of speeds.

questions.stem: A velocity-time graph is a straight segment from 5 m/s at t = 0 to 11 m/s at t = 3 s. Use the graph slope to identify a, use its rectangle-plus-triangle area to find displacement, and show how the same graph yields v = u + at, s = ut + 0.5at^2, and v^2 = u^2 + 2as.

answer.summary: The slope gives a = 2 m/s^2 and v = u + at. The graph area is 15 m + 9 m = 24 m, giving s = ut + 0.5at^2. The trapezoid form combined with t = (v-u)/a gives v^2 = u^2 + 2as.
reasoning: Slope: a = (11-5)/3 = 2 m/s^2, so a = (v-u)/t rearranges to v = u + at.
Rectangle area: u t = 5 x 3 = 15 m.
Triangle area: 0.5(v-u)t = 0.5 x 6 x 3 = 9 m, so s = 24 m; substituting v-u = at gives s = ut + 0.5at^2.
The same area is s = 0.5(u+v)t. Substitute t=(v-u)/a: 2as=(u+v)(v-u)=v^2-u^2, hence v^2=u^2+2as.
answer.check: The direct displacement validator gives 24 m, and 11^2 = 5^2 + 2 x 2 x 24 = 121.

hints.text: Start with the two graph invariants: slope is acceleration, and velocity-time area is displacement.
Split the area into u t plus 1/2(v-u)t; then use the slope relation v-u=at.

questions.stem: A runner moves uniformly around a circular track of radius 7 m and completes one revolution in 14 s. Find the speed, then state the qualitative directions of velocity and acceleration at any point.

answer.summary: The speed is pi m/s, about 3.14 m/s. Velocity is tangent to the circle in the direction of motion; acceleration points inward toward the centre.
reasoning: One revolution covers circumference 2 pi r = 14 pi m.
v = 14 pi m / 14 s = pi m/s ≈ 3.14 m/s.
Constant speed does not make velocity constant because its direction changes.
The velocity is tangent and the turning acceleration is inward.
answer.check: Doubling the period at the same radius would halve the speed, while the tangent/inward direction distinction remains.

hints.text: One complete revolution covers the circle circumference, 2 pi r.
Divide that path length by the revolution period for the constant speed.

questions.stem: On a velocity-time graph, velocity changes from +3 m/s at 2 s to +5 m/s at 4 s. Find the average acceleration over that interval and state what a horizontal velocity-time segment would mean.

answer.summary: Average acceleration is +1 m/s^2. A horizontal velocity-time segment means zero acceleration over that interval.
reasoning: Delta t = 4 - 2 = 2 s.
a_avg = Delta v / Delta t = +1 m/s^2.
A horizontal velocity-time segment has Delta v = 0, so its average acceleration is zero.
answer.check: The result matches the positive slope of the displayed velocity-time segment.

hints.text: Read the vertical axis first: this graph shows velocity, not position.
Average acceleration is signed velocity change divided by elapsed time.

questions.stem: Design the inclined-plane motion practical needed to produce both a distance/position-time graph and a velocity-time graph. State what you measure, how you construct the two graphs, and what graph evidence would support approximately constant acceleration.
conditions: Use one trolley/body moving down one fixed incline and one declared positive direction.

answer.summary: Measure position along the incline at known times, plot position against time, calculate interval velocities from successive position changes over time changes, plot those velocities against representative times, and look for an approximately straight velocity-time trend whose slope is approximately constant.
reasoning: Use time as the horizontal variable and measured distance/position along the incline as the first vertical variable.
Keep the same origin, direction and units for every reading.
Estimate interval velocity from Delta x / Delta t for successive measurements and associate each value with its interval or midpoint time.
Plot the velocity estimates against time; an approximately straight trend indicates approximately constant acceleration over the tested interval.
Repeat trials or use multiple readings so a single timing error does not determine the conclusion.
answer.check: The position-time graph and velocity-time graph must be built from the same motion data and use increasing time coordinates; graph slope, not graph height, carries the rate interpretation.

hints.text: Start with a table of time and position along the incline; both graphs must come from measured motion data.
Use successive Delta x / Delta t values to build the velocity-time data before interpreting its slope.

questions.stem: A ball is projected vertically upward from a marked launch point with speed u. Choose upward as positive and treat the local gravitational acceleration magnitude g as constant. Derive the time to the highest point and the maximum height above the launch point.
conditions: u>0 and g>0.
Air resistance is neglected.
The represented height interval uses the local constant-g approximation.

answer.summary: With +up, the signed acceleration is a=-g. At the highest point v=0, so t_top=u/g. Using v^2=u^2+2as gives H=u^2/(2g).
reasoning: Declare +up once, so the initial velocity is +u and gravity is a=-g.
At the apex use only the event condition v=0; acceleration remains -g.
From v=u+at, 0=u-g t_top, hence t_top=u/g.
From v^2=u^2+2as, 0=u^2-2gH, hence H=u^2/(2g).
answer.check: Both results increase with launch speed; stronger local g shortens the rise time and reduces the maximum height.

hints.text: After choosing +up, which signed value must the downward gravitational acceleration have for the whole rise?
At the top use v=0 as the event condition, then choose one relation for time and one that eliminates time for height.

questions.stem: A stone is released from rest at height h above the ground. Put the origin at the release point and choose upward as positive. Find the time to reach the ground and the signed velocity just before impact.
conditions: h>0 and g>0.
Air resistance is neglected.
Use the local constant-g approximation.

answer.summary: The ground is at s=-h, u=0 and a=-g. From -h=-(1/2)gt^2, the future impact time is t=sqrt(2h/g). The impact velocity is v=-gt=-sqrt(2gh).
reasoning: With the origin at release and +up, the ground displacement is -h and gravity is a=-g.
Use s=ut+0.5at^2 with u=0 to obtain -h=-0.5gt^2.
Time for the future event is the positive root sqrt(2h/g).
Then v=u+at=-gt, giving the negative impact velocity -sqrt(2gh).
answer.check: The negative velocity means downward in the declared +up coordinate; changing the coordinate direction would change signs, not the physical impact speed.

hints.text: With the origin at release and +up, what is the signed displacement of the ground?
Use u=0, s=-h and a=-g; select the positive time root because the question asks for a future impact.

questions.stem: A ball is projected vertically upward from a marked point with speed u and later returns to the same point. Choose upward as positive. Find the nonzero return time, the signed return velocity, the whole-trip displacement, and the whole-trip distance.
conditions: u>0 and g>0.
Air resistance is neglected.
Local g is treated as constant.

answer.summary: For the return event s=0 with a=-g. The nonzero solution of 0=ut-(1/2)gt^2 is t=2u/g. The return velocity is v=u-gt=-u. Whole-trip displacement is 0, while total distance is 2H=u^2/g.
reasoning: The return point equals the launch point, so signed displacement for the whole trip is zero.
Solve 0=ut-0.5gt^2: t=0 is the launch event and t=2u/g is the later return.
Substitute the later time into v=u-gt to obtain v=-u.
Maximum height is H=u^2/(2g), so path length up plus down is 2H=u^2/g.
answer.check: The final speed equals the launch speed in this ideal model, but the velocity sign reverses; zero displacement does not mean zero distance.

hints.text: Returning to the launch point fixes the signed displacement, not the total path length.
Set s=0 in the constant-acceleration displacement equation and keep the nonzero future-time root.

questions.stem: A stone is released from rest h above the ground, but this time choose downward as positive and put the origin at the release point. Find the signed acceleration, ground displacement, time to impact and signed impact velocity.
conditions: h>0 and g>0.
Air resistance is neglected.
Use the same physical drop as an ordinary free-fall case.

answer.summary: With +down, a=+g and the ground is at s=+h. The impact time is sqrt(2h/g) and the signed impact velocity is +sqrt(2gh). These describe the same physical drop as a +up solution with negative s, a and v.
reasoning: The downward physical gravity direction now agrees with the positive axis, so a=+g.
The ground is h units in the positive direction, so s=+h.
From h=0.5gt^2, t=sqrt(2h/g).
Then v=gt=+sqrt(2gh).
answer.check: The impact time and speed are coordinate-invariant; only the signs of directed quantities change when the axis is reversed.

hints.text: The sign of g follows the declared axis. Does downward gravity align with or oppose a downward-positive coordinate?
Use s=+h and a=+g consistently; compare the final physical speed with the +up representation afterward.

questions.stem: A ball thrown vertically upward reaches its highest point. Choose upward as positive. State the instantaneous velocity and acceleration at the top, then describe the signs of velocity just before and just after that instant.
conditions: Air resistance is neglected.
Local g is treated as constant and positive in magnitude.

answer.summary: At the top v=0 but a=-g. Just before the top v>0; just after the top v<0. The downward acceleration does not vanish or reverse at the turning point.
reasoning: The highest point is the instant when the upward velocity has decreased to zero.
Gravity still points downward, so with +up the acceleration remains -g.
A moment before the apex the ball moves upward, giving positive velocity.
A moment after it moves downward, giving negative velocity.
answer.check: A horizontal tangent through v=0 on a position-time graph would not imply zero acceleration; a velocity-time graph crosses zero with slope -g.

hints.text: Does the gravitational interaction disappear at the instant the velocity reaches zero?
Compare velocity signs just before and after the top while keeping the gravitational acceleration direction fixed.

questions.stem: A ball is physically launched upward with speed u from the origin, but a solver deliberately chooses downward as positive. Write the signed initial velocity and acceleration, derive the signed displacement to the highest point and the time to reach it, and show that the physical maximum height agrees with the usual +up calculation.
conditions: u>0 and g>0.
Downward is the declared positive direction.
The physical launch remains upward.

answer.summary: With +down, initial velocity is -u and acceleration is +g. At the top v=0. From 0=u^2+2g s_top, s_top=-u^2/(2g), so the physical height is |s_top|=u^2/(2g). From 0=-u+gt, t_top=u/g.
reasoning: The physical upward launch opposes the downward-positive axis, so u_signed=-u.
Gravity aligns with the axis, so a=+g for the whole flight.
Use v=0 at the top without changing a.
The top lies in the negative coordinate direction, giving negative signed displacement but positive physical height.
answer.check: The coordinate signs differ from a +up solution, but t_top and physical height are identical.

rubric.criterion: Assigns u_signed=-u and a=+g under the downward-positive convention.
rubric.evidence_of: Transforms directed quantities with the coordinate choice rather than with verbal up/down rules.

rubric.criterion: Obtains a negative signed displacement to the apex.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeps the apex physically above an origin whose positive axis points downward.

rubric.criterion: Recovers the same positive physical height and top time as the +up representation.
rubric.evidence_of: Checks coordinate invariance of the physical event.

adaptation.reason: Reverses the coordinate axis while holding the physical upward launch fixed, forcing a signed representation translation rather than a memorized -g rule.

hints.text: With downward positive, what signs represent an upward initial velocity and a downward acceleration?
Use the same apex condition v=0, then interpret a negative displacement as a physical point above the origin.

transfer.statement: The learner must translate the same physical vertical throw into the opposite coordinate convention and verify that physical height and time remain unchanged.

questions.stem: A ball is launched vertically upward from a balcony with speed u. The ground is H below the launch point. Put the origin at the balcony and choose upward as positive. Derive the future time at which the ball reaches the ground and the signed impact velocity.
conditions: u>0, H>0 and g>0.
Air resistance is neglected.
Use the bounded constant-g model.

answer.summary: The ground event has s=-H and a=-g, so -H=ut-(1/2)gt^2. The future root is t=[u+sqrt(u^2+2gH)]/g. The signed impact velocity is v=u-gt=-sqrt(u^2+2gH).
reasoning: The origin is at launch and +up, so the ground has negative displacement -H.
Insert s=-H, initial velocity +u and a=-g into the displacement equation.
The quadratic has one negative-time root and one positive future root; keep the positive root.
Substitute that time into v=u-gt, or use v^2=u^2+2gH and choose the negative sign because impact motion is downward.
answer.check: When H tends to zero, the future return time tends to 2u/g and the impact velocity tends to -u, matching return to the launch level.

rubric.criterion: Uses s=-H with +up and keeps a=-g throughout.
rubric.evidence_of: Represents the changed origin/event without changing the gravity sign.

rubric.criterion: Chooses the positive future-time root from the quadratic.
rubric.evidence_of: Interprets algebraic roots as physical events.

rubric.criterion: Reports a negative impact velocity under +up.
rubric.evidence_of: Uses motion direction to interpret the square-root sign without altering acceleration.

adaptation.reason: Changes release from rest into an upward launch from an elevated origin, requiring a quadratic future-event selection while preserving the same signed-gravity model.

hints.text: With the launch point as origin and +up, what signed displacement names the ground event?
The displacement equation produces two algebraic roots; keep the one that represents a time after launch.

transfer.statement: The learner must carry the same constant-g sign model through a changed origin and choose the physically relevant future root for an impact event below the launch point.

questions.stem: A ball projected vertically upward with speed u passes a point h above the launch level once on the way up and once on the way down. Choose upward as positive. Compare the two velocities at that same height without first solving for the two times.
conditions: Air resistance is neglected.
Local g is constant over the flight.

answer.summary: At displacement s=+h, v^2=u^2-2gh. Therefore the two passages have the same speed sqrt(u^2-2gh) but opposite signed velocities: +sqrt(u^2-2gh) on ascent and -sqrt(u^2-2gh) on descent.
reasoning: Use the no-time constant-acceleration relation with a=-g and the same displacement +h for both passages.
The equation determines v^2, so it fixes speed magnitude but not direction.
The ascent event has positive velocity under +up.
The descent event has negative velocity under +up.
answer.check: Equal height does not mean equal velocity; the signs differ even though the speed magnitudes agree in this ideal model.

rubric.criterion: Uses the same signed displacement +h for both passages.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizes that position is identical even though motion direction differs.

rubric.criterion: Obtains one common value for v^2.
rubric.evidence_of: Uses the no-time relation without forcing a direction prematurely.

rubric.criterion: Assigns opposite signs to ascent and descent velocities.
rubric.evidence_of: Distinguishes equal speed from equal velocity.

adaptation.reason: Changes the endpoint from the launch level to an intermediate height visited twice, requiring the learner to separate same position and same speed from same signed velocity.

hints.text: At the two passages the displacement from launch is the same, but is the direction of motion the same?
Use the relation containing v squared to get the common speed magnitude, then assign velocity signs from ascent versus descent.

transfer.statement: The learner must interpret a squared-velocity result at one position visited twice, preserving equal speed while assigning opposite velocity directions.

questions.stem: A solver chooses upward as positive for a vertical throw. They use a=-g until the ball reaches the top, then change to a=+g because the ball is moving downward. Decide whether this model change is valid and state the correct signed acceleration before, at and after the apex.
conditions: The same upward-positive axis is retained throughout.
Air resistance is neglected.
Local gravitational acceleration is treated as constant.

answer.summary: The model change is invalid. With one fixed +up axis, gravity is downward at all three stages, so a=-g before the apex, a=-g at the apex and a=-g after the apex. Velocity changes from positive through zero to negative; acceleration does not reverse.
reasoning: The coordinate axis is fixed, so a physical downward vector always has a negative signed component.
Gravity does not reverse when the object's velocity reverses.
At the apex v=0 only instantaneously while a remains -g.
After the apex velocity becomes negative under the same negative acceleration.
answer.check: Changing to +g while keeping +up would describe an upward physical acceleration after the apex, contradicting the gravity model.

rubric.criterion: Rejects the acceleration-sign flip while the axis remains fixed.
rubric.evidence_of: Makes acceleration sign depend on the coordinate convention and physical direction, not velocity direction.

rubric.criterion: Keeps a=-g at the apex despite v=0.
rubric.evidence_of: Separates instantaneous velocity from acceleration.

rubric.criterion: Distinguishes the sign change of v from the unchanged sign of a.
rubric.evidence_of: Represents the turning point correctly.

adaptation.reason: Changes from a consistent alternate axis to an inconsistent mid-flight sign switch, testing whether the learner selects acceleration sign from the fixed coordinate convention rather than the direction of velocity.

hints.text: Did either the positive axis or the physical direction of gravity change when the ball passed through the top?

transfer.statement: The learner must reject a familiar but invalid acceleration-sign switch when velocity reverses, preserving one signed gravity model across the turning point.

questions.stem: A ball is launched vertically upward from its starting level with speed u. Choose upward as positive. Describe the velocity-time graph from launch until the ball first returns to the launch level, and use the graph to identify the apex time and return time.
conditions: Air resistance is neglected.
Local g is constant and positive in magnitude.
Only the interval from launch to first return is considered.

answer.summary: The v-t graph is a straight line starting at +u with constant slope -g. It crosses v=0 at t=u/g, the apex, and reaches v=-u at t=2u/g, the first return to launch level. Positive and negative triangular areas cancel, giving zero net displacement over the whole interval.
reasoning: Constant signed acceleration a=-g makes velocity decrease linearly with time.
The zero crossing occurs when 0=u-gt, so t=u/g.
The return event has equal positive and negative v-t areas because net displacement back to the start is zero.
The straight line therefore reaches -u at t=2u/g.
answer.check: The graph slope stays -g through the zero crossing; a horizontal slope at the apex would incorrectly imply zero acceleration there.

rubric.criterion: Describes one straight v-t line of slope -g across ascent and descent.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeps constant gravitational acceleration through the direction reversal.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the zero crossing at u/g as the apex.
rubric.evidence_of: Translates the turning-point event into graph form.

rubric.criterion: Uses equal positive/negative areas or the linear relation to place the return at 2u/g with v=-u.
rubric.evidence_of: Connects graph representation to signed displacement and the return event.

adaptation.reason: Changes a local before/top/after turning-point description into a full velocity-time representation whose slope, zero crossing and signed areas encode the same constant-g flight.

hints.text: With constant a=-g, what shape must a velocity-time graph have, and what does its slope represent?
Use the zero crossing for the apex; for return to the starting level, the signed area under v(t) over the whole interval must be zero.

transfer.statement: The learner must translate the same vertical constant-g motion into a velocity-time graph, preserving the nonzero slope at the apex and using signed area for the return event.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg mass moves at 4.0 m/s in a horizontal circle of radius 2.0 m on a single ideal string. In an inertial frame, identify the horizontal force arrow(s) on the mass and calculate the required inward net force.
conditions: Ignore air resistance.
Treat the string interaction as the only horizontal physical force.

answer.summary: Draw tension only, directed inward. The required net radial force is m v^2/r = 16 N, so the string tension supplies 16 N horizontally in this model. Do not add a second centripetal-force arrow.
reasoning: The string is the only horizontal physical interaction.
Centripetal names the inward resultant role, not another force.
answer.check: Tension + Fc would double-count the same inward requirement.

hints.text: List physical agents before writing the radial equation.
Use inward-positive Sigma F_r=m v^2/r.

questions.stem: A 1000 kg car takes a flat circular curve of radius 50 m at 10 m/s. With mu_s=0.30 and g=10 m/s^2, decide whether static friction can supply the required inward force without slipping. Do not assume f_s=mu_s N unless the threshold is reached.
conditions: Road is horizontal.
No other horizontal force is modeled.
Use N=mg for this horizontal no-vertical-acceleration state.

answer.summary: Required inward friction is m v^2/r=2000 N. The static limit is mu_s N=0.30*10000=3000 N, so no-slip is feasible and actual static friction is 2000 N, below its maximum.
reasoning: Compute the radial demand first.
For the flat no-vertical-acceleration model N=mg=10000 N.
Compare 2000 N with the bound 3000 N.
Because demand is below the bound, static friction self-adjusts to 2000 N.
answer.check: Using 3000 N as the actual friction at 10 m/s would produce too much inward acceleration for the stated radius.

adaptation.reason: Changes the inward-force mechanism from a single string tension to self-adjusting static friction with a capacity boundary.

hints.text: First calculate the inward force the motion requires; only then compare it with the static-friction limit.

transfer.statement: The learner must separate the required radial friction from the maximum available static friction and select no-slip only if the demand is within the bound.

questions.stem: A mass on a taut string moves in a vertical circle of radius r. Write the radial force equation at the top and at the bottom using inward positive at each point. Then obtain the minimum top speed for the just-taut boundary.
conditions: String is massless and taut except at the limiting top case.
Ignore air resistance.

answer.summary: Top: T+mg=m v_top^2/r. Bottom: T-mg=m v_bottom^2/r. At the just-taut top boundary T=0, mg=m v_min^2/r, so v_min=sqrt(gr).
reasoning: At the top inward is downward, so T and mg are both positive radial contributions.
At the bottom inward is upward, so T is positive and mg negative.
A string cannot push, so the limiting taut top state is T=0.
Solve the top equation for the nonnegative speed.
answer.check: mv^2/r is the required net radial force, not another force added to T and mg.

adaptation.reason: Changes the radial axis orientation and force combination around a vertical circle, then adds the physical tension boundary.

hints.text: Redraw the inward arrow separately at the top and bottom before assigning signs.

transfer.statement: The learner must re-declare the radial positive direction at two positions and derive a boundary from T=0 instead of memorizing a minimum-speed formula.

application_contexts.title: Bounded vertical one-dimensional motion under local gravity
application_contexts.description: A one-dimensional vertical-motion context in one inertial frame, with air resistance neglected and local gravitational acceleration treated as constant over the represented height interval.
invariants: Choose one vertical positive direction and keep it for the whole represented interval.
Use g>0 for the local gravitational-acceleration magnitude; the signed acceleration follows from the chosen axis.
Gravity points downward throughout the bounded flight even when velocity changes direction.
At a turning point the instantaneous velocity may be zero while gravitational acceleration remains nonzero.
The constant-g model is a bounded local approximation and does not claim that g has one universal value everywhere.
